planting.note: Plant small container-grown specimens in spring into lean, gravelly, sharply drained soil, since like most brooms this species dislikes root disturbance once established.

directions: Corsican broom is a dense, intensely spiny mound-forming shrub endemic to Corsica and Sardinia, where it grows on rocky, sun-baked maquis slopes. In late spring it carries a heavy flush of small, bright yellow, pea-shaped flowers that are notably fragrant, making it a favorite of specialist rock-garden and alpine nurseries. It demands lean, fast-draining soil and full sun, and is intolerant of winter wet or heavy, rich ground. Once established it is extremely drought tolerant and resents being transplanted after its taproot has formed, so site it carefully from a young plant.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew — Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring or fall into lean, sharply drained, gritty soil in full sun, mimicking the rocky coastal ground of its native range.

directions: This subshrubby spurge is native to rocky coastal habitats of Corsica, Sardinia, and the Balearic Islands, forming low clumps of narrow, glaucous blue-green leaves on woody-based stems. In spring it produces the typical euphorbia display of yellow-green bracted flower clusters above the foliage, adding cool color and texture to dry gravel and Mediterranean-style gardens. It tolerates salt spray and poor, rocky soil but needs sharp drainage to avoid winter rot in wetter climates. CAUTION: like other euphorbias, its milky latex sap is a skin and eye irritant, so wear gloves when cutting back old growth.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew — Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Start seed indoors in late winter or plant divisions outdoors after frost danger passes, into lean, well-drained soil in full sun.

directions: Cyprus oregano is a low, woody-based culinary herb native to Cyprus and parts of the eastern Mediterranean and Levant, closely related to the marjorams within the genus Origanum. Its small, soft, grey-green leaves carry a pungent, warm oregano-like flavor and are used fresh or dried in local cooking much as common oregano is used elsewhere. It produces small white to pale pink flower clusters in summer that attract pollinators. Grow it in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun, since like other Mediterranean oreganos it is prone to rot in damp, heavy, or overly fertile ground.

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in a hot, sheltered, sharply drained site, since this Crete native resents both winter wet and hard frost.

directions: Cretan ebony is a striking low shrubby legume endemic to the island of Crete, prized by dry-garden and rock-garden specialists for its dense covering of silky, silver-white hairs on both stems and leaves. In late spring and early summer it sends up dense, bottlebrush-like spikes of bright pink to magenta pea flowers that contrast dramatically with the silvered foliage. It needs a hot, sun-baked position with very sharp drainage, such as a raised bed, wall crevice, or gravel garden, and is markedly less cold-hardy than most Mediterranean rock-garden plants, often needing winter protection or a very sheltered microclimate outside mild coastal climates.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew — Plants of the World Online
